To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

stereotype threat can influence the motivational experiences of underrepresented students by disrupting achievement goal orientations and sense of belonging and decreasing intrinsic motivation, which, in turn, can lead to lower performance, less persistence, and less domain identification.

1) ST influences achievement orientations, sense-of-belonging, and intrinsic motivation; 2) ST influences achievement goal orientations, sense-of- belonging, and intrinsic motivations through the mediating role of self-regulation; and 3) ST influences achievement goals, sense-of- belong, and intrinsic motivation through the mediating roles of stereotype threat and self-regulation.
stereotype threat influences the motivational experiences and behaviors of students who are stereotyped in a domain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether ST is a temporary or chronic experience that influences stigmatized students over the long-term.
the question of how ST influences the motivational experiences of stigmatized students over time.
how ST influences stigmatized students' motivational processes and how these motivational processes influence their academic and career outcomes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
stereotype threat is a significant barrier to the achievement of minorities in education.
the motivational experience model of ST is a useful framework that can help to explain the effects of ST in a variety of contexts.

stereotype threat is a powerful force in education and it can have long term negative effects on students’ learning and motivation, and it is important to consider stereotype threat when trying to understand students’ learning and performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the negative effects of ST are not just limited to the performance domain.
ST is a self-regulatory experience that can be managed through self-regulation strategies, such as self-affirmation and self-efficacy, as well as by the social environment.
ST influences the motivational experiences of stigmatized students, particularly through the achievement goal and sense of belonging domains.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the negative effects of ST extend beyond the moment of performance to the long-term maintenance of academic and career motivation.
the negative effects of ST on performance, self-efficacy, and other outcomes are only the tip of the iceberg.

ST is a self-regulatory process that can be understood in terms of the motivational experiences that it engenders, and that such experiences have important implications for the long-term persistence, engagement, and performance of stigmatized students.
